questions.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}y={x}^{2}{y}^{2}
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution* $z={y}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{z}{x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}{x}^{2} \\ -\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-{x}^{2}z & =-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-{x}^{2},\,Q(x)=-{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}-{x}^{2}z) & ={e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}\cdot (-{x}^{2}) \\ {e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}\cdot \frac{dz}{dx}-{e}^{{x}^{3}/3}{x}^{2}z & =-{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}/3} \\ \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}) & =-{x}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-{x}^{3}/3})\,\,dx & =-\int {x}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}\,dx \\ z{e}^{-{x}^{3}/3} & ={e}^{-{x}^{3}/3}+C \\ z & =1+C{e}^{{x}^{3}/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =1+C{e}^{{x}^{3}/3} \\ y & =\frac{1}{1+C{e}^{{x}^{3}/3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order Initial Value Problem Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y+3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{x},\,y(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation*

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z=-3x
$$

*using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z=-3x.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)\,.
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-3x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-3x) \\ x\cdot \frac{dz}{dx}+z & =-3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dx}(xz) & =-3{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(xz)\,dx & =-\int 3{x}^{2}\,dx \\ xz & =-{x}^{3}+C \\ z & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{C-{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition $y(1)=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{C-1}\,⟹\,C=2\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{2-{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a First-Order Linear ODE Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-2}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y(1-x{y}^{2})
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{-3/2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{-3/2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{z}^{-1/2}(1-x{z}^{-1}) \\ {z}^{-3/2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}{z}^{-1/2}(x{z}^{-1}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}z(x{z}^{-1}-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z & ={x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)={x}^{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order Initial Value Problem Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
(x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}=2{y}^{1/2}(x+1)^{3}+2y,\,y(0)=\frac{1}{4},\,x>-1.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(0)=\sqrt{y(0)}=\frac{1}{2}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x+1},\,Q(x)=(x+1)^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/(x+1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)^{-1}} \\  & =(x+1)^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>-1.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=(x+1)^{-1}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,z & =x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int (x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\,z & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C \\ z & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(0)=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(0) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (0+1)(\frac{1}{2}{0}^{2}+0+C) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2}) \\ y & =(x+1)^{2}{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,,\,x>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x})+{z}^{-1} & ={x}^{2}{({z}^{-1})}^{2} \\ -\frac{x}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{z} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{z} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{z}{x} & =-x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}\,z & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/xdx} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x{|}^{-1}} \\  & =|x{|}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot (-x) \\ \frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}z & =-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{z}{x}] & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{z}{x}]\,\text{d}x & =\int -1\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z}{x} & =-x+C \\ z & =-{x}^{2}+Cx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =-{x}^{2}+Cx \\ y & =\frac{1}{Cx-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
